absent: Expiry cache layout, inactivity encoding, and sampling helpers for thread and group CPU time
Contracts of thread and process collection helpers and firing list ownership beyond what handling shows
Timer fire action, signal delivery, overrun accounting, and nanosleep wakeup mechanics
Timer lifecycle helpers for create, set, delete, get, rearm, expiry query, and retry code conditions
Task work queueing flags, execution context guarantees, and mutex lifetime rules
CPU clock identifier encoding, per thread extraction, and scheduler clock definition
Restart block type values, remaining time copyout, and signal pending interaction with schedule
Ktime and timespec conversion helpers and monotonic to real mapping details
Security hook for time setting, vsyscall zone publication, warp logic, and device randomness effects
Timekeeping forward, NTP interfaces, leap source, ktime data refresh, cycle conversion, vsyscall, VDSO aux, and pvclock chain contracts
Read base and fast keeper layouts, sequence and latch primitives, and action flag and keeper identity encodings
Jiffies update rules, tick context, interrupt disable guarantees, and lockdep assertion meanings

findings.text: Tick expiry probe for POSIX CPU timers is available to timer tick path. It assumes disabled interrupts and current task context and internally decides between immediate handling and deferred task work.

Per task CPU timer work control can be reset to a clean unscheduled state with fresh callback association and mutex initialization. One variant serves copied task state and one serves early boot initialization of the initial task.

Wall time and zone setting services are provided for system paths. One accepts an optional calendar value plus optional zone info, the other accepts a calendar value alone. Both validate before applying.
A timespec normalization helper is provided that carries whole seconds between second and nanosecond fields until the subsecond field lies in canonical range.

Three clock operation tables expose CPU clock behaviour. The generic POSIX CPU table offers resolution, set, read, timer lifecycle, sleep, rearm and wait operations. Process and thread tables offer small subsets delegating to the generic logic with fixed clock identities.

Tick entry requires interrupts disabled, abandons work when the current task is exiting, skips when deferred work is already marked scheduled, skips when fast heuristic reports no expiry, otherwise dispatches to the configured expiry runner.
Task work entry runs in task context for the current task, serializes concurrent expiry handling with the per task mutex, then invokes the central timer handling routine.

CPU clock sleep entry rejects sleeps that name the current thread through a per thread identifier, otherwise performs a temporary timer sleep and arranges restart handling for relative sleeps while absolute sleeps use a distinct restart error.
Stub clock set entry only honors the realtime identifier, copies the requested value from user space, then delegates to the shared settimeofday logic.
Thread local expiry is probed only when the expiry cache is not marked inactive. Sampling and expiry evaluation occur on demand and a positive result requests full handling.

Group expiry is treated as a lock free heuristic using activity and in progress markers read without sighand protection. Sampling uses an atomic group time source. Deadline overrun independently forces handling even when no timer appears expired.

While sighand is held, collection of thread and process expiries refreshes the expiry cache and the cache stays consistent because no queue or modify operation can interleave. The repeat loop is vacuous for direct interrupt expiry and meaningful only for deferred task work expiry.

Deferred work reenable distinguishes kernel configurations. Without realtime preemption it simply clears the scheduled marker because no tick could interleave. With realtime preemption it disables interrupts, rechecks for newly expired timers when time advanced, and requests another collection pass when needed.

Deferred dispatch warns once when invoked while already marked scheduled and otherwise marks scheduled and queues task work with resume semantics. The direct dispatch variant instead invokes handling synchronously bracketed by lockdep markers and never uses the scheduled marker.

Timers moved to the private firing list are protected by a per timer firing marker. After sighand release each timer is locked individually, unlinked, its marker cleared and sampled, an event is generated only when the sampled marker still indicates firing, and the handling pointer is cleared.

Waiting for concurrent expiry pins the recorded handling task, drops read side protection to allow blocking, briefly holds that task expiry mutex to join completion, then releases the reference and restores read side protection. A trivial configuration instead only relaxes the processor.

Nanosleep uses a stack timer initialized empty with negative overrun and sleep marking, armed with the requested interval. It sleeps interruptibly until expiry or signal, treats vanished expiry as success, and on signal disarms, queries remaining time, retries deletion while concurrent handling is reported, and reports either success when already fired or a restartable sleep error.

Sleep restart reenters the sleep as an absolute wait using the stored expiry converted to calendar form and the stored clock identity. Process and thread clock identities alias the scheduler clock for identifier zero and their operations delegate to generic CPU clock helpers.

Settimeofday validates the calendar value, consults a security hook, constrains zone offset to a bounded range, publishes zone state to low level readers, performs a one time clock warp for zone only initialization, and delegates calendar changes to the timekeeper setter.

Wall time application forwards the keeper to now, computes the delta between requested and current wall time, rejects deltas that would invert the monotonic offset, otherwise shifts the wall to monotonic offset and installs the new wall value, publishes from shadow, then notifies timer, audit and entropy consumers.

Wall to monotonic installation first checks that the stored real offset matches the negated monotonic offset, then stores the new monotonic value and publishes derived real and TAI offsets with ordered writes paired with lock free readers.

Shadow restore copies live state to shadow while holding the keeper lock. Shadow publish brackets updates with a write sequence, optionally clears NTP state, refreshes leap and ktime derived data, derives the real base, propagates by keeper kind, optionally bumps the set sequence, writes seconds first for torn read safety, then copies the full keeper and closes the sequence.

Coarse subsecond cache mirrors the shifted mono nanosecond field. Wall read combines stored seconds with shifted nanoseconds and wall install updates seconds, shifted nanoseconds and coarse cache together. Fast keeper publication uses a latch sequence to move readers between two buffer slots while each slot is updated in turn. Leap refresh obtains the next leap instant and rebases it to monotonic unless marked absent. Auxiliary keeper detection is either a range test or a constant false by configuration.

Collection holds sighand with interrupt state saved. Sighand is released before acquiring any per timer lock to avoid inversion. Per timer handling uses a plain spin lock, justified because expiry runs either in hard interrupt context or in task work where all other timer lock users are task context.

Task work expiry is serialized by a per task mutex. Concurrent waiters pin the handling task under read side protection, drop that protection to block on the same mutex, then reacquire protection to balance the call site. The sleep specific waiter additionally drops and reacquires the timer irq lock around the block.

Wall installation and shadow operations require the timekeeper lock with interrupt state saved. Readers are fenced by a write sequence covering low level and keeper updates together, and fast readers are fenced by a latch sequence covering the double buffer.

Nanosleep arming, expiry polling, disarm and deletion occur under the timer irq lock, which is dropped across voluntary schedule and across waits for concurrent handling, then reacquired before further timer state inspection.
Per task work control comprises a task work item bound to the CPU timer work handler, a mutex serializing expiry, and a boolean scheduled marker distinguishing queued from idle states.

CPU timer state comprises list linkage for queue membership, a firing marker for collection ownership, a handling pointer identifying the task performing expiry, a sleep marker for temporary nanosleep timers, and an expiry value queried to distinguish fired from armed states.

Timekeeper time state comprises wall seconds, a mono read base holding shifted nanoseconds, a coarse nanosecond cache, wall to monotonic offset, derived real and TAI offsets, next leap instant, NTP error and tick adjustment, keeper identity, and a clock was set sequence counter.
Restart sleep state comprises a clock identity, a stored expiry instant, and a sleep type distinguishing absent from armed sleeps. Remaining time is reported through a calendar interval value.
Fast timekeeping state comprises a latch sequence plus two read base slots. Readers select a stable slot via the latch while writers update slots one at a time around latch transitions.

Timer expiry moves from queued to collected to firing listed under sighand, then to unlinked and marker cleared under per timer lock, then branches to event generation when firing persisted or silent drop when a concurrent rearm or delete cleared it, ending with handling pointer clearance.

Deferred expiry moves from idle to scheduled on queue, to handling under mutex in task work, to reenable where it either returns to idle or repeats collection when realtime ticks introduced new expiries during the pass.

Nanosleep moves from init to armed to waiting, then to success when expiry vanishes, or to interrupted when a signal arrives, then to disarmed with remaining time captured, with a retry subloop while deletion reports concurrent handling, ending in success, restartable sleep, or setup error.

Wall setting moves from validation to locked shadow preparation with time forwarded, to delta computed, to rejected when monotonic would invert or accepted with offsets and wall installed, to published with sequence fenced propagation, to post notification for timers audit and entropy.

Fast publication moves readers off the slot under update, updates the first slot, latches readers back, updates the second slot, then closes the latch, giving readers a consistent view without blocking.

Because group activity markers are observed without locks, a thread may miss a concurrent activation or completion and defer group expiry until another member observes it on a later tick. The design accepts this delay as analogous to normal signal delivery jitter.

On realtime kernels ticks can interleave collection because sighand does not suppress interrupts, so reenable must detect time advance and recollect. Concurrent rearm or delete can clear the firing marker after collection, requiring the sampled marker test before event generation, and exiting tasks must be pinned to avoid missing a firing timer during deletion.

Publishing low level time state before the keeper without fencing readers could expose time appearing to step back. Publishing the keeper with a torn copy could expose corrupt seconds. The design fences with a write sequence and orders seconds before the full copy to keep second granularity readers safe.

A wall request far behind current time could invert monotonic time if applied naively. The setter rejects such deltas by comparing against the current wall to monotonic offset. Zone values outside the allowed range are likewise rejected before publication.
Fact: stub clock set accepts only CLOCK_REALTIME. Fact: other identifiers yield EINVAL and user copy failure yields EFAULT.
Fact: zone offset in minutes must stay within plus or minus fifteen hours. Fact: normalization keeps nanoseconds inside NSEC_PER_SEC by whole second carry and borrow.

Fact: temporary sleep timers start with overrun negative one and sleep marking set. Fact: per thread sleep naming the caller yields EINVAL. Fact: TIMER_ABSTIME selects absolute timing. Fact: interrupted relative sleeps yield ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK with restart arranged while absolute sleeps yield ERESTARTNOHAND. Fact: PROCESS_CLOCK and THREAD_CLOCK alias CPUCLOCK_SCHED for identifier zero.
Fact: absent leap uses KTIME_MAX and skips rebasing. Fact: auxiliary keeper test uses TIMEKEEPER_AUX_FIRST and TIMEKEEPER_AUX_LAST in one configuration and constant false in the other.
